lead: A protocol is a precise agreement on how two entities exchange messages. A standard records that agreement so many vendors can build compatible products. Layering hides the details of lower layers, letting each layer focus on a single function and speak a uniform protocol to the layer above. This makes network devices from different makers interoperate, and lets engineers design, test, and upgrade parts of a network independently. Layered models are used in every modern data‑communication system, from a home Wi‑Fi router to the backbone of the Internet.
prereq: You need: basic data‑communication concepts from Chapter 1.1.

blocks.text: A protocol defines the syntax, semantics and timing of messages exchanged between two communication entities. Syntax is the format of bits; semantics is the meaning of each field; timing is the order and speed of exchange. A standard is a publicly documented protocol that a standards body maintains. It ensures that any product following the standard can interoperate with any other product that also follows it.

items: ISO (International Organization for Standardization) publishes the OSI model and many link‑layer standards.
IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) defines Ethernet (IEEE 802.3) and Wi‑Fi (IEEE 802.11).
IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) publishes RFCs such as TCP (RFC 793) and IP (RFC 791).

blocks.text: Only a few universities call this topic "protocol layering" in their syllabus, but it appears in almost every networking course worldwide.

Layering separates concerns. The physical layer worries only about voltage levels, the data‑link layer about framing and error detection, the network layer about routing, and so on. Each layer communicates with the one above using a service‑access point (SAP) and receives data in a protocol data unit (PDU). By hiding lower‑layer details, an application developer can write code without knowing the exact wiring of the network.

items: A layer receives a PDU from the layer below.
It removes the header added by that lower layer.
It processes the payload and adds its own header.
It passes the new PDU to the next higher layer.

blocks.where: Payload is the original data in bytes; Header_i is the header size added by layer i.

blocks.text: The formula shows that the total size grows linearly with the number of layers that add headers. This growth is why designers try to keep header sizes small.

Consider the message "Hi" which is 2 bytes. It must travel through three layers: Application, Transport and Network. Each layer adds a 2‑byte header. Using the formula above, the final frame size is 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8 bytes.

blocks.code:
payload = 2
header_per_layer = 2
layers = 3
frame = payload + layers * header_per_layer
print(frame)

blocks.text: If a layer forgets to add its header, the frame would be only 6 bytes. That mistake is a common exam trap.

examples.question: A payload of 2 bytes is sent from an application to the network. The Application, Transport and Network layers each add a 2‑byte header. Compute the size of the final frame that leaves the Network layer.
steps: Final frame size = Payload + Total header size = 2 bytes + 6 bytes = 8 bytes.
examples.answer: The final frame size is 8 bytes.
examples.check:
payload = 2
layers = 3
header = 2
frame = payload + layers * header
print(frame)

traps: Forgetting that each layer adds its own header, leading to an underestimate of the frame size.
Mixing up header size (bytes) with header length (bits) and forgetting to convert.
Assuming the Network layer does not add a header because IP is sometimes called a "routing protocol".

quiz.a: A set of rules that defines the format, meaning and timing of messages exchanged between two entities.

quiz.q: Why are standards needed in networking?
quiz.a: Standards document protocols so that equipment from different vendors can interoperate, allowing a market of compatible products.

quiz.q: A file of 1500 bytes is transmitted through a four‑layer stack. Each layer adds a 20‑byte header. What is the size of the transmitted frame?
quiz.a: Payload = 1500 bytes; total header = 4 × 20 = 80 bytes; frame size = 1500 + 80 = 1580 bytes.

quiz.q: If a layer adds a 2‑byte header but the designer forgets to include it, how many bytes short is the final frame compared to the correct size?
quiz.a: The frame will be 2 bytes short because one header is missing.

quiz.q: Explain how layering helps in upgrading a network without changing applications.
quiz.a: Applications use the service offered by the transport layer. If the transport layer is replaced with a newer protocol that offers the same service interface, applications need not change. The lower layers (network, data‑link, physical) can also be upgraded independently because each layer communicates with its neighbor through a defined interface.

quiz.q: Name three standard‑setting bodies mentioned in this chapter.
What does the acronym PDU stand for and what is its role in a layered architecture?
quiz.a: Protocol Data Unit; it is the packet of data that a layer passes to the layer above after adding its own header.

quiz.q: A network engineer argues that adding more layers makes a protocol slower. Using the frame‑size formula, discuss the validity of this claim.
quiz.a: More layers increase the total header overhead, which can enlarge frames and cause more transmission time, especially on low‑bandwidth links. However, the processing delay of each layer is usually small compared to transmission delay, and the benefits of modular design often outweigh the slight speed loss.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, layered architectures enable micro‑service networking and software‑defined networking where each function can be virtualised. Research explores flattening layers to reduce latency for ultra‑low‑delay applications such as high‑frequency trading. For the next step, study how the TCP/IP suite maps its four layers to the OSI model and experiment with custom protocol headers using tools like Scapy.
